title: Very Late‐Onset Myasthenia Gravis Presenting With Dysphagia and Gradual Decrease in Laryngeal Elevation During Repeated Swallowing: A Case Report
case_prompt: A 72‐year‐old man presented with a 1.5-month history of progressive dysphagia and a 10-kg weight loss. His medical history was notable for lung cancer resected 6 years earlier and Parkinson’s disease diagnosed 3 years ago, with residual mild festinating gait. On examination, he appeared moderately wasted but not anemic. Neurologic assessment showed a weakened pharyngeal reflex and dysphagia on water‐swallowing testing; limb strength was normal, but balance was impaired (Barthel Index 80, Berg Balance Scale 38, MMSE 28). An upper gastrointestinal radiograph demonstrated decreased tongue‐base mobility, delayed pharyngeal swallow initiation, insufficient laryngeal elevation and upper esophageal sphincter opening, and a gradual decrease in laryngeal elevation during repeated swallows. Chest CT showed right upper-lobe atelectasis with bronchiectasis and bilateral pneumonia. Based on these findings, myasthenia gravis could not be excluded, and electromyography was planned.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Cerebrovascular disease was considered due to acute bulbar dysfunction — “These symptoms often need to be differentiated from cerebrovascular disease and motor neuron disease.”  
2. Motor neuron disease was considered given progressive dysphagia — “These symptoms often need to be differentiated from cerebrovascular disease and motor neuron disease.”  
3. Parkinson’s disease–related dysphagia was considered because of his Parkinson’s history but was less likely, as “this is different from the characteristics observed in dysphagia caused by MG and can be used for differentiation.”  
4. Paraneoplastic syndrome was considered given his history of lung cancer but deemed unlikely since “the relief and improvement of symptoms occurred independently of any antitumor interventions, making a paraneoplastic syndrome unlikely in this case.”  
5. Myasthenia gravis was favored based on bulbar‐pattern findings on radiography and the inability to exclude MG — “MG could not be excluded.”
